title: An ode to the work no one claps for
summary: Discover why the most valuable enterprise technology often goes unnoticed – and how governance, orchestration and AI help keep critical systems working.
body_markdown:
You know that feeling when you’re about to miss a train you’ve spent hundreds of dollars on? I do. I forgot to forward my Amtrak ticket to my phone from my work email last month. So I sat down on the floor of Penn Station, iced coffee sweating in my hand, and sorted it out in two minutes flat. I even caught the train with three minutes to spare. The ticket scanned. Nothing went wrong. It was another Monday.


But behind every one of those moments – the card that cleared, the ticket that scanned, the train that pulled out of the station at exactly 7:03 AM – were thousands of people working quietly to make sure my Monday worked out just fine. Yours too, probably. You’ll never meet most of them. You probably don't know they exist. But that’s exactly the point.


## We've confused flashiness with importance.


We live in a world that rewards visibility. The attention economy has trained us to believe that if you're not being seen, you're not winning. Every headline competes to be more outrageous than the last. Every product launch is a revolution. Every AI announcement is the one that changes everything. As a millennial, I've developed full immunity to "once in a lifetime" events. Forever wars, financial crises, a global pandemic, bonkers political shifts. We've had enough historic moments for several lifetimes and somehow they keep coming.


How this constant stream of noise is changing us is borne out in the data. According to the 2026 Edelman Trust Barometer, only 47% of Americans trust major institutions – business, government, media, NGOs – with the UK at 44% and France at 42%. Just 32% of global respondents believe the next generation will be better off. The mood is bleak, and the doom scroll never ends.


But here’s my fundamental belief: There’s a lot of hope available if you go looking for it. And the overwhelming majority of what keeps the world running has nothing to do with what makes the news. We've optimized so hard for what's loud that we've become blind to what's load-bearing.


## The invisible infrastructure is everywhere if you know where to look.


A few months ago, my colleague, Emma, had a nice day out. When she got home and turned in for the night, she started experiencing increasingly alarming back symptoms. A feeling of cold water trickling down her spine, as well as numbness in her limbs. Around 11:30 PM, she called NHS 24's emergency line and within about half an hour was triaged, assessed, and set up with a doctor’s appointment at eight the next morning. What she didn't know at the time was that the clinical decision support system fielding her call was[built on Pega](https://www.pega.com/insights/resources/nhs-24-builds-foundation-care-patients-can-trust) . She actually works for the company that, in some weird, roundabout way, helped her heal.


I love this story because it perfectly captures something that's genuinely hard to articulate: The world is held up by an intricate web of people and systems that most of us will never see, who care deeply, and are working daily to make sure things just... work. And when things just work, they feel boring.


This is one of the biggest paradoxes in modern tech: Invisibility is its own form of excellence. The flashiest software update with the most jaw-dropping demo always gets the stage time. The methodical implementation that kept the lights on across a national health service, quietly handling millions of calls, governed and predictable and clinically safe? That one rarely gets the limelight. But ask anyone who's called a health line at 2 AM whether they'd rather have a wow-factor portal or a system that actually works. You already know the answer.


NHS 24 isn't the only example. The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs[uses Pega](https://www.pega.com/insights/resources/pegaworld-inspire-2024-department-veterans-affairs-keynote-caring-more-our) to manage the crushing volume of medical paperwork for veterans living abroad – people who've served their country and now have to navigate bureaucracy from thousands of miles away. It's not a flashy use case. No one's writing think pieces about VA paperwork. But for a veteran sitting in Manila or Frankfurt waiting on a benefits decision so they can schedule an MRI, it's no small thing.


## What this means if you're building for the enterprise right now.


We're deep in what many are calling the SaaS-pocalypse: an era of massive AI hype, tool proliferation, and the creeping anxiety that if you're not moving 30X faster, you're already behind. Enterprise leaders are being pressured from every direction – boards demanding AI adoption, teams stretched across fragmented systems, risk surfacing too late, and a very real fear of public failure when execution breaks.


The leaders who will actually win aren't the ones chasing every new capability. They're the ones asking: *When everything can act, build, and decide – who's actually in charge when outcomes matter?*


The organizations that hold up are the ones that build with intent. Not just speed, but governance. Not just automation, but orchestration. The emerging competitive advantage isn't being first to deploy, but being the one with a solution that still works at scale, six months later, when no one is watching.


## So here's what I want to leave you with.


Notice the invisible army. It's there every time a system works the way it should, every time an outcome holds when the pressure is on, every time someone on the other end of a phone line knows exactly what to do next. There are thousands of people and organizations doing that work right now, unglamorous and unannounced.


Maybe you're already one of them. Maybe in a roundabout way, you're building the infrastructure that you yourself will rely on, without ever knowing it.


If you want to experiment with building that way intentionally,[Pega Blueprint](https://www.pega.com/blueprint) is a good place to start.
